blocks.intro_md:
Since the 2023 edition, large language models and related AI tools have become part of how many people read and search Jewish texts. This section gathers tools that are useful for serious study and research, developer resources for building such tools, and a selection of scholarship and essays on AI and Judaism.

AI tools are good at some tasks: finding passages when one does not know the exact wording, suggesting parallels and later discussions, adding vocalization, expanding abbreviations, giving a first draft of a translation, and turning manuscript images into searchable text. Tools that retrieve passages from a fixed library and link every claim to its source are much more reliable than general chatbots that answer from memory.

The main risk is invented or wrong citations. Models produce sources that do not exist, attach real quotations to the wrong work, and summarize a sugya or responsum with confidence and in error. Treat every AI answer as a lead, not a finding: open the cited source, read it in context, and check the edition and wording before relying on it. Machine transcriptions and translations need the same check against the original.

Tools in this field change quickly. Status notes record what was checked on 9-Oct-2026; several projects found in the source lists were already offline.

entries.name: Sefaria: AI features and Library Assistant
entries.summary: Sefaria's page on its AI features, including an experimental chatbot that answers with linked citations, and its rules for labeling AI content.
entries.annotation_md:
- The page sets out where Sefaria uses AI: LLM-based citation linking (also through the Sefaria Linker on outside sites), AI-assisted introductions and source selection on about 1,000 English topic pages, a Pirkei Avot learning guide drafted by AI and reviewed by staff, relevance sorting of user source sheets, and an AI-drafted, human-edited English translation of the Kli Yakar.
- The **Library Assistant**, an experimental chatbot built on Claude that answers questions with cited, linked sources, launched in spring 2026.
- Policy points: AI content is marked (an outline star for AI-assisted content with human review, a filled star for unreviewed AI content); AI output must point back to sources in the library; AI is not used for halakhic rulings or personal advice.
entries.status_note: Checked live 9-Oct-2026. The sefaria.org URL redirects by language (e.g. to sefaria.org.il).

entries.name: Mekoros
entries.summary: AI source-finder that collects primary sources on a Torah topic, traces how an idea developed, and exports source sheets.
entries.annotation_md:
- Covers Tanakh, both Talmuds, Rishonim, Acharonim, halakha and responsa; built on the Sefaria library.
- States that each result is checked against the primary text. How this check works is not described, so treat it as a claim and verify quotations yourself.
- A pricing page exists; the free scope was not confirmed.

entries.name: Binata
entries.summary: Hebrew-first AI study assistant that answers with source references and marks quotations it cannot match to the original text.
entries.annotation_md:
- Library: Tanakh and commentaries, Bavli and Yerushalmi, midrash, Rishonim, Shulchan Arukh with commentaries, and responsa; draws on Sefaria. Subscribers can add their own texts.
- Each quotation is checked against the source; unmatched quotes are flagged as unverified. A "research mode" writes a longer article.
- Free monthly quota for registered users; premium subscription in shekels. Interface mainly Hebrew, with an English option. Presents itself as a study aid, not a halakhic authority.

entries.name: Ituria
entries.summary: Open-source AI agent that searches a Jewish text library, reads passages and pulls commentaries before it answers.
entries.annotation_md:
- Uses a reason-and-act agent design with a local full-text index and the Sefaria API. Built in connection with the Otzaria project.
- Works with several model providers (Claude, GPT, Gemini) or local open models through Ollama.
- Code on GitHub; a demo is linked from the README.

entries.name: Torah Research Board
entries.summary: Infinite-canvas research workspace that places Sefaria texts side by side with AI analysis.
entries.annotation_md:
- A Sefaria "team pick" in the Powered by Sefaria list.
- The site is a JavaScript app; details of the AI model and its citation handling could not be checked automatically.
entries.status_note: Site responds (9-Oct-2026); features not verified in detail.

entries.name: Yochai
entries.summary: Socratic AI study partner that leads the user to primary sources and asks questions rather than giving answers.
entries.annotation_md:
- Built on a curated library of more than 1,000 primary sources with entity data linked to Sefaria.
- Developed by Zohar Atkins (per jewishai.me).
entries.status_note: Site responds (9-Oct-2026); described as a "Jewish Learning Companion".

entries.name: PshatGPT
entries.summary: Tap a line of Talmud or Tanya to get a streamed AI explanation of its plain meaning in context.
entries.annotation_md:
- Covers the Babylonian Talmud and Tanya (more Hasidic works announced); texts come from Sefaria. Offers several explanation styles and longer "iyun" sessions.
- Daily free limit; beyond it users can supply their own Anthropic API key.
- Explanations are model output, not a commentary: check them against Rashi and the standard commentaries.
entries.status_note: Checked live 9-Oct-2026. Page notes a move to a new home and that account sync was not yet configured.

entries.name: Dicta tools (2026 update)
entries.summary: Dicta's free machine-learning tools for Hebrew texts, including automatic vocalization, abbreviation expansion and citation finding.
entries.annotation_md:
- Also listed in the 2023 guide (Dicta entry under Search and Related Tools). Tools most relevant here:
    - [Nakdan](https://nakdan.dicta.org.il/): adds nikud automatically; modes for modern, rabbinic and poetic Hebrew.
    - [Rabbinic abbreviation expander](https://abbreviation.dicta.org.il/): resolves ראשי תיבות in context.
    - [Citation finder](https://citation.dicta.org.il/): finds exact and loose quotations of Bible, Mishnah and Talmud in a pasted text.
- Dicta, led by Moshe Koppel, also publishes open language models (see the Dicta Hugging Face entry below).

entries.name: Sofer.ai
entries.summary: AI platform for Torah media: transcribes shiurim in mixed English, Hebrew, Yiddish and Aramaic, and converts scanned Hebrew and Rashi-script books to text.
entries.annotation_md:
- Transcripts have timestamped topic outlines and click-to-play audio; a search tool ("Maishiv") answers only from the user's own transcripts and notes.
- OCR for scanned Hebrew and Rashi script.
- Free tier (a few transcripts a month) and paid personal and commercial plans.
- Founded by Zachary Fisch; see the Seforim Chatter interview under Readings.

entries.name: MiDRASH (ERC Synergy project)
entries.summary: Large European-Israeli project to transcribe and analyze tens of thousands of medieval Hebrew-script manuscripts with HTR and NLP.
entries.annotation_md:
- Full title: "Migrations of Textual and Scribal Traditions via Large-Scale Computational Analysis of Medieval Manuscripts in Hebrew Script" (ERC grant 101071829). Partners: EPHE-PSL (Paris), Tel Aviv University, Bar-Ilan University, with the National Library of Israel and the University of Haifa.
- Targets about 30,000 manuscripts and 300,000 fragments in Hebrew, Aramaic and Judeo-Arabic; uses NLI KTIV images and the eScriptorium/kraken toolchain (see Escriptorium in the 2023 guide).
- First outputs are on Zenodo (next two entries). A conference on computational manuscript studies is planned at Tel Aviv University in December 2026.

entries.name: MiDRASH automatic transcriptions of the Cairo Geniza
entries.summary: Downloadable first-pass machine transcription of the National Library of Israel's entire Cairo Geniza image collection.
entries.annotation_md:
- Released November 2025 (CC BY 4.0), a zipped text file of about 445 MB; made with kraken. Fragments are matched to KTIV by their system number.
- The publishers call it "very preliminary and imperfect": segmentation and reading errors, some wrong reading order, vertical text mostly skipped, weaker Arabic-script results. Use it to find fragments, not to quote them.
- Corrected transcriptions are to be added to KTIV.

entries.name: MiDRASH Geniza HTR model
entries.summary: Open handwritten-text-recognition model for Hebrew-script Geniza fragments, for use with kraken and eScriptorium.
entries.annotation_md:
- Fine-tuned on documentary and literary Geniza texts (including Tannaitic literature and Talmud) on top of a broad Hebrew-script base model. Abbreviations are not expanded.
- Version 2, February 2026; license CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

entries.name: Transkribus: Hebrew and Yiddish models
entries.summary: Transkribus page listing its public Hebrew-script recognition models and the option to train a model on one's own manuscripts.
entries.annotation_md:
- Public models include DiJeSt 3.0 (printed Hebrew and Yiddish; see the 2023 entry on the DiJeSt model), a 15th-century Sephardic semi-cursive model, the Pinkas Brody model for 19th-century communal records, and several Yiddish handwriting models.
- No general public model for medieval Ashkenazi or Italian hands was found; for such material users usually train their own model (about 50-150 transcribed pages).
- Free monthly credits; paid plans for larger work.

entries.name: Tikkoun Sofrim
entries.summary: Crowdsourcing project in which volunteers correct machine transcriptions of medieval Hebrew manuscripts of Midrash Tanhuma.
entries.annotation_md:
- Joint project of the University of Haifa, the National Library of Israel and EPHE (Paris). Manuscripts were first read with kraken; each line is corrected by several volunteers and the best reading is chosen automatically.
- Reported character error rates of about 3-9% before correction, on manuscripts in Paris, Parma, the Vatican and Geneva.
- Described in the ACM *Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage* (2021). A forerunner of the MiDRASH work.
entries.status_note: Project blog found via web search 9-Oct-2026; current activity not confirmed.

blocks.subsection: Developer resources: APIs, MCP servers, models and datasets

entries.name: Sefaria developer portal and API
entries.summary: Documentation and interactive reference for Sefaria's free API, with links to its data exports, Hugging Face assets and MCP servers.
entries.annotation_md:
- API reference: [developers.sefaria.org/reference](https://developers.sefaria.org/reference/getting-started).
- An [llms.txt](https://developers.sefaria.org/llms.txt) index lists the docs in Markdown and the endpoints in OpenAPI form, for use by AI agents.
- The [Powered by Sefaria](https://developers.sefaria.org/docs/powered-by-sefaria) page lists more than 130 projects built on the API.

entries.name: Sefaria MCP servers
entries.summary: Official Model Context Protocol servers that let AI assistants such as Claude or ChatGPT search and quote the Sefaria library with citations.
entries.annotation_md:
- **Sefaria Texts MCP** connects an assistant to the library for text questions with cited answers; **Sefaria Developers MCP** helps write code against the API.
- Tools include text retrieval, search, links between texts, dictionary search, bibliographic data and manuscript images.
- Open source: [Sefaria/sefaria-mcp](https://github.com/Sefaria/sefaria-mcp). Docs last updated September 2026.
- An assistant connected this way can still misread or over-summarize a text; the gain is that its quotes come from the library and can be checked.

entries.name: Sefaria Linker
entries.summary: Script for websites that finds citations of Jewish texts on a page and links them to Sefaria; now uses LLMs to recognize references.
entries.annotation_md:
- Sefaria's AI page describes the Linker as using LLMs to identify citations both inside the library and on outside websites.
- Sefaria's open citation-recognition models are on its Hugging Face page.
entries.status_note: Checked live 9-Oct-2026. The sefaria.org URL redirects by language.

entries.name: Torah MCP
entries.summary: Community MCP server for Claude that adds a chavruta mode, citation discipline and full-text search of about 50,000 HebrewBooks volumes to Sefaria access.
entries.annotation_md:
- Open source (MIT). Sixteen free tools, including Sefaria text search, HebrewBooks search, calendar and gematria.
- The site itself recommends using it together with Sefaria's official MCP server.

entries.name: Torah Scholar (agent skill)
entries.summary: Small open-source skill and command-line tool that lets AI agents search Sefaria and fetch texts, links and commentaries.
entries.annotation_md:
- Commands for search, verse lookup, links and related texts; uses the Sefaria API with no key.
- Core features free; a paid add-on unlocks extra features.

entries.name: Ask the Rambam: RAG tutorial
entries.summary: Beginner-level video tutorial on building a retrieval-augmented Q&A bot that answers only from the Mishneh Torah.
entries.annotation_md: - A worked example of the main technique behind citation-grounded tools: retrieve passages first, then let the model answer only from them.

blocks.subsection: Developer resources: APIs, MCP servers, models and datasets

entries.name: Sefaria on Hugging Face
entries.summary: Sefaria's open models and datasets: citation and named-entity recognition models, full library exports, links and Hebrew-English pairs.
entries.annotation_md:
- Models: Hebrew and English Torah NER, reference and sub-reference recognizers, and a BEREL-based linker model.
- Datasets: Hebrew and English library dumps, the links graph, Rabbinic Hebrew-English pairs, a gold NER set, and the Rabbinic Embedding Leaderboard (next entry).

entries.name: Rabbinic Embedding Leaderboard
entries.summary: Benchmark results comparing text-embedding models on retrieving and matching rabbinic Hebrew and Aramaic passages.
entries.annotation_md:
- About 3,700 test pairs across Talmud, Mishnah, Midrash Rabbah, halakha and other categories; scores for 32 models (results dated January to September 2026).
- Useful for anyone choosing an embedding model for semantic search over rabbinic texts. MIT license.

entries.name: Sefaria Export
entries.summary: Full bulk download of the Sefaria library (about 26 GB) in JSON, plain-text and CLTK formats, with schemas and the links graph.
entries.annotation_md:
- Files are in a public cloud bucket; the repo holds a monthly-updated index (books.json) and download scripts.
- Licenses vary by text version; check each text's license before reuse.

entries.name: Dicta on Hugging Face (DictaLM, DictaBERT, BEREL)
entries.summary: Dicta's open Hebrew language models: the DictaLM chat models, DictaBERT encoders and BEREL for rabbinic Hebrew.
entries.annotation_md:
- **DictaLM 3.0** (late 2025): open-weight Hebrew-English chat models in 24B, 12B and 1.7B sizes, Apache-2.0.
- **DictaBERT**: encoders for segmentation, morphology, syntax, lexical tasks and vocalization.
- **BEREL** (BERT Embeddings for Rabbinic-Encoded Language, 2022): a model trained for rabbinic Hebrew; BEREL 3.0 is the newer version.
- Most are for developers; the Nakdan and other Dicta web tools put them to use for end users.

blocks.subsection: Developer resources: APIs, MCP servers, models and datasets

entries.name: Hebrew and Arabic NLP resources (NNLP-IL)
entries.summary: Searchable directory of Hebrew and Arabic NLP corpora, models and tools, with license information.
entries.annotation_md:
- Mostly modern Hebrew, but includes rabbinic and historical items such as BEREL, the Sefaria export, Project Ben-Yehuda dumps, JPress and the KIMA historical gazetteer.
- Run by Israel's National NLP Program.
